title: From Source Text to Tokens
text: From Source Text to Tokens A compiler usually begins by grouping characters into tokens. A token has a category, such as NUMBER, IDENTIFIER, or PLUS, and may preserve the original spelling as its lexeme. For the input total + 42, a lexer might emit IDENTIFIER("total"), PLUS("+"), and NUMBER("42"). The lexer should prefer the longest valid match when token rules overlap. Whitespace is commonly discarded, but its source position can still be recorded for diagnostics.

title: Parsing Expressions
text: Parsing Expressions A parser turns a token sequence into structure. Precedence determines which operator binds more tightly, while associativity resolves repeated operators at the same precedence level. For 1 + 2 * 3, multiplication binds more tightly than addition, so the tree represents 1 + (2 * 3). A recursive-descent parser can encode this by giving each precedence level its own function. Useful parser errors report the unexpected token, its source location, and a small set of expected token categories.

title: Token Design Exercise
text: Token Design Exercise Design token categories for a tiny calculator language containing decimal integers, names, +, -, *, /, parentheses, and assignment. Explain how your lexer handles count2, 12abc, ==, and an unknown character. Do not write a full lexer. Describe the rules, their priority, and two focused test cases.
